title: Occupancy sensitivity to input-length distribution: Nsight runs and CUDA-graph interaction
content:
Purpose:
This doc records an investigation into how the distribution of input sequence lengths (not just mean length) affects GPU occupancy, perceived utilization, and tail latency in our inference runtime. We suspected that long-tail length distributions cause CUDA graph fragmentation, KV-cache hot paths, and more frequent kernel-launch gaps, reducing realized SM occupancy even if theoretical occupancy (per-kernel) remains high.

High-level hypothesis:
- When a workload has a wide length distribution (mix of very short and very long requests) the runtime’s batching and CUDA-graph reuse patterns fragment, causing:
  * More kernel launch points (short-lived kernels for short requests interleaved with long kernels), increasing CPU-side launch jitter.
  * Reduced effective occupancy because microbatches often end early and leave SMs underutilized while other warps are waiting for KV-cache loads.
  * Amplified tail latency due to stream synchronization and kernel preemption/queue ordering effects.

Test environment:
- Model: LLaMA-2-13B-8bit (quantized int8 path used in production experiments)
- Hardware: 8x A100 80GB (single GPU per run), CUDA 12.2, cuDNN 9.x, Nsight Systems 2024.3
- Runtime: serving-runtime commit 1a2b3c (branch: input-length-experiments)
- Key flags toggled: cuda_graphs_enabled=true/false, persistent_kernels=true/false, stream_priority=normal/high, kv_cache_prefetch=true/false
- Microbatching: logical batch sizes tested: 1, 4, 8; physical microbatch horizon = 32 tokens
- Workload shapes:
  1) Narrow short: 80% 8-token, 20% 16-token (median 8)
  2) Narrow long: 80% 256-token, 20% 128-token (median 256)
  3) Bimodal mix: 50% 8-token, 50% 256-token (wide distribution)
  4) Heavy-tail: Pareto with alpha=1.6 truncated [8,1024] (captures rare 1% very long requests)
- Metrics captured: SM utilization (per Nsight), Achieved occupancy (hardware counters), active warps per SM, kernel duration distribution, kernel launch latency (CPU->GPU), CUDA graph reuse counts, KV cache hit ratio, P99/P95 latency, throughput

Methodology:
- For each workload shape run 3 10-minute steady-state Nsight recordings after warming (2 minutes warm-up).
- Repeat with cuda_graphs_enabled=true and false to isolate graph reuse effects.
- Collect detailed kernel timelines, aggregated histograms of kernel durations, and per-kernel occupancy reports.
- Also measured CPU-side batching queues to detect scheduling jitter.

Key observations (aggregated):
1) Baseline narrow-short workload:
   - Nsight: SM utilization ~72% steady, achieved occupancy reported ~78% on hot kernels, active warps per SM near theoretical.
   - CUDA graphs provided ~1.15x throughput improvement, launch overhead negligible.
   - P99 latency stable ~42ms (batch=4).

2) Narrow-long workload:
   - SM utilization higher for long-lived kernels (~82%); kernels are long and steady, GPU saturation good.
   - CUDA graphs maximize reuse; graph cache hit ~94%.
   - Throughput good, P99 ~120ms (expected due to longer decode).

3) Bimodal mix (50/50 short/long) — the surprising case:
   - Overall SM utilization dropped to ~54% observed by Nsight.
   - Per-kernel achieved occupancy for long kernels unchanged (~80%) but short kernels showed low achieved occupancy (~28%). Short kernels were frequently launched interleaved with long kernels causing stream stalls and small serialization points.
   - CUDA graph reuse fell to ~62% because graphs compiled for long-trace shapes weren't reused for short-request microbatches; runtime created distinct graphs and evicted them more often.
   - Kernel launch latency histogram developed a heavy tail — small kernels experienced queueing delays of 100-300us more frequently.
   - Effective throughput decreased by ~18% vs an equivalent aggregated-latency expectation. P99 latency increased by ~35% compared to narrow-short.

4) Heavy-tail workload (Pareto):
   - Behavior interpolates the bimodal case but with worse tails: occasional very long requests created long-lived kernels that occupied SMs for many ms, during which many short requests queued and executed in small, fragmented kernels.
   - Nsight timelines show repeated short-kernel bursts between long kernels, with visible gaps of underutilized SMs (dark stripes) corresponding to microbatch boundaries and stream synchronization points.
   - CUDA graph cache churn was high; graphs compiled for long sequences dominated memory and caused eviction of short-sequence graphs, more graph recompile thrash.

Microbatching and KV-cache interactions:
- When kv_cache_prefetch=true we observed a modest improvement for mixes because prefetching reduces per-step KV loads, increasing short-kernel durations slightly and improving occupancy by ~6 percentage points in the bimodal case.
- However, prefetch increases memory pressure; on GPUs with tight memory budgets this caused more frequent paging in other tests.

Impact of CUDA graphs toggles:
- cuda_graphs_enabled=true helps when workload shapes are stable (narrow long or narrow short) since compiled graphs map closely to the runtime executions.
- For wide distributions, graphs introduce a cache management problem: cached graphs tailored to long traces crowd out graphs for short traces and vice versa. The runtime’s current graph eviction policy (LRU by allocation time) is not workload-aware and causes suboptimal reuse.

Root causes (analysis):
- The runtime batches requests by arrival and forms microbatches keyed by sequence-length buckets. In wide distributions, many microbatches end up heterogeneous and the runtime chooses to split/repack, resulting in partial microbatches and frequent kernel boundary crossings.
- Short kernels have poor per-kernel utilization because their work size is small relative to SM capacity; when interleaved with long kernels the scheduler shows visible preemption and stream serialization effects.
- CUDA graph cache churn magnifies the problem: graph compile latency and eviction cause increased CPU-side handling and graph warm-up kernels (fallback launch paths) that further reduce occupancy.

Actionable mitigations tested (and notes):
1) Length-aware batching window (prototype): hold short requests (up to X ms) to pack them into fuller microbatches or to coalesce with other short requests only — reduced occupancy loss in bimodal case by ~9 p.p. but added small median latency (~6ms) for short requests.
2) Graph fingerprinting by "shape class" not exact sequence: compile and index graphs by discrete sequence-length buckets (8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512) rather than full token-by-token signature — graph reuse improved from 62%->88% in wide cases and P99 improved by ~20%.
3) Short-kernel slow-path batching: fallback path that groups many short sequences into a single kernel specialized to small sequence lengths, optimizing thread/block config for higher occupancy. Reduced short-kernel achieved occupancy from 28%->50% in tests.
4) KV-cache prefetch heuristics: enable only for GPUs with >X free memory and when KV hit ratios are expected high; otherwise leave off. This avoids memory pressure tradeoffs.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Optimal graph eviction policy: should be workload-aware (frequency * cost) rather than pure LRU. Need sim/trace-based modeling and a simple heuristic to start.
- Microbatch hold-window sizing: what is the best tradeoff point globally? Need production A/B on low-traffic customers to measure UX impact.
- Can we implement a compact multi-shape graph that supports dynamic sequence termination without full recompilation? (investigate templated graphs or parameterized graphs)
- Effect on multi-GPU setups with NVLink/KV coherence: we ran single-GPU tests; results may differ when KV cache coherence across NVLink induces different access patterns.

Recommended next steps (priority):
1) Ship graph-bucketing (shape classes) as an opt-in runtime flag for the next canary build (low-risk, big win).
2) Implement short-kernel aggregation slow-path and enable behind opt-in flag.
3) Add telemetry: graph cache hit ratio per shape-class, microbatch-size histogram, and per-request wait times to detect length-distribution issues in production.
4) Create a synthetic workload generator for bimodal/heavy-tail shapes and add to CI performance tests.

Appendix: quick reproduction steps
- Checkout branch input-length-experiments (commit 1a2b3c)
- Run packed test script: tools/perf/run_length_sweep.sh --model llama2-13b-int8 --gpu 0 --shape bimodal --duration 600 --microbatch 32 --cuda-graphs true/false
- Collect Nsight: nsight-sys --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=bimodal-2025-03-12.qdrep --target-processes all --stop-on-duration 600
- Postprocess: tools/perf/parse_nsight.py --qdrep bimodal-2025-03-12.qdrep --metrics sm_util,achieved_occupancy,active_warps,kernel_launch_latency

Notes to reviewers:
- The raw Nsight captures (nsight://session/2025-03-12-01) are large; I left an extracted CSV in GCS: gs://redwood-perf/2025-03/occupancy-length-bimodal.csv
- This is an early draft; I prioritized experiments that expose mechanisms rather than exhaustive tuning. Comments welcome on prioritization and how to roll mitigations into canary vs experiment flags.

Maya Patel
Senior SWE, Serving Runtime
